name: Automattic Inc.
origin_detail: Founded 2005 by Matt Mullenweg, who co-founded the WordPress open-source project in 2003, to monetize WordPress; distributed/remote company based in San Francisco
openness_notes: WordPress and Automattic's main plugins (WooCommerce, Jetpack) are GPL; the business is hosting (WordPress.com), commerce and services, plus some proprietary apps (Tumblr, Day One). WordPress trademarks were transferred to the WordPress Foundation in 2010, but the 2024 WP Engine dispute showed that WordPress.org infrastructure is effectively controlled by Mullenweg personally, so governance is not neutral (not level 4).

license_history.license: GPL unchanged; source code and trademarks transferred to the WordPress Foundation
license_history.note: Governance/trademark step, not a licence change

license_history.license: ACF plugin forked as 'Secure Custom Fields' (GPL) on WordPress.org
license_history.note: 12 Oct 2024: WP Engine's Advanced Custom Fields replaced in the directory using the same slug, so users were switched on update

risk_events: Sep 2024: Mullenweg called WP Engine 'a cancer to WordPress', demanded trademark royalties, and WordPress.org banned WP Engine (25 Sep 2024)
2 Oct 2024: WP Engine sued Automattic and Mullenweg (extortion, abuse of power, Computer Fraud and Abuse Act claims)
Oct 2024: 159 employees (8.4%) took a severance offer for disagreeing with Mullenweg's stance
12 Oct 2024: ACF plugin taken over/forked as Secure Custom Fields
10 Dec 2024: preliminary injunction ordered Automattic and Mullenweg to restore WP Engine's access to WordPress.org
Feb 2025: class action by a WP Engine customer against Automattic and Mullenweg
9-12 Sep 2026: board placed Mullenweg on paid leave and named CFO Mark Davies interim CEO; Mullenweg regained control within ~33 hours; co-founding CEO Toni Schneider reportedly left the board
robustness: WordPress itself is very robust (GPL, huge ecosystem, Foundation-held trademarks), and could be forked if the steward misbehaves. Automattic as a company has shown governance fragility: founder-centric control of WordPress.org, a costly trademark war, staff departures, a 16% layoff and a failed 2026 board attempt to remove its CEO. No priced round since the 2021 $7.5B valuation was found.
physical_science_relevance: Low directly; WordPress powers many lab, department and project websites.
openness_effect_assessment: GPL licensing made WordPress the dominant web CMS and let a whole hosting industry (including WP Engine, backed by Silver Lake since 2018) profit from it, which Automattic came to view as free-riding. Its attempt to extract royalties via trademark and control of WordPress.org infrastructure, instead of relicensing, triggered lawsuits, an injunction, community distrust and internal turmoil, showing that informal control of 'open' infrastructure is itself a risk.
key_takeaway: Automattic shows that a fully GPL product with weak neutral governance can turn a free-rider complaint into a governance crisis: the code stayed open, but the steward used trademarks and the plugin directory as leverage, leading to litigation (2024-2025) and a 2026 boardroom fight. Openness built a $7.5B (2021) company; personal control of the commons put it at risk.
